title: AI-Powered Espionage Campaign Targets Government Linux Infrastructure
summary: Our analysis an AI-powered espionage campaign targeting government Linux infrastructure with custom malware, web shells, and advanced credential theft.
body_markdown:
## Executive Summary


Unit 42 identified a campaign targeting government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure, with observed activity spanning from October 2025–April 2026. We track this activity as CL-UNK-1211.


In the operations we witnessed, the attackers relied on AI-generated payloads. Multiple artifacts deployed throughout the intrusion contained AI-made conversational annotations and developer reasoning comments, suggesting that the code was either generated using large language models (LLMs) or executed by an automated AI agent.


The attackers behind this cluster of activity focused on Linux environments to conduct extensive reconnaissance and maintain persistent network access to support intelligence-gathering. The attackers attempted to dump sensitive databases and exfiltrate government mailboxes to access social media accounts.


The campaign included a diverse toolkit that combined open-source tools, custom cross-platform backdoors and widespread web shell deployments. We observed various defense evasion techniques, including attempts to disable endpoint protections, erase system logs and plant deceptive red-team markers to disguise activity as a legitimate security assessment.


Our attribution of this activity to CL-UNK-1211 is in accordance with the[Unit 42 attribution framework](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/unit-42-attribution-framework/) . We designate the term UNK to clusters of activity whose affiliation with either nation-state or cybercrime activity we have not yet determined.


This investigation uncovers the defining tools, techniques and attack patterns of this activity cluster.

## Technical Analysis Overview


Our analysis of the CL-UNK-1211 cluster of activity reveals a versatile operational playbook tailored to enterprise Linux and database environments. The attackers targeted government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure, maintaining persistent access by using a combination of custom cross-platform backdoors, open-source utilities and widespread web shell deployments.


The attackers enumerated mailboxes to identify and gain access to social media accounts tied to government email addresses. In addition, they dumped entire database contents before attempting to exfiltrate the data.


The attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 exhibited a methodical approach to defense evasion. This included attempting to disable endpoint protections on compromised systems, and to tamper with system logs that might contain evidence of the attack.


We provide a comprehensive analysis of the defining tools, techniques and procedures (TTPs) used throughout the operation, highlighting how the attackers leveraged AI to streamline payload creation across their execution workflow. Our analysis details key mechanisms across the attack chain. These include:


- Initial access via web shell deployment and credential harvesting
- Custom RAT execution
- Mailbox targeting
- Anti-forensics measures


## Using AI to Streamline Payload Creation


Throughout the operation, the attackers relied on malicious PHP and shell scripts to maintain persistence, perform reconnaissance and exfiltrate data. These payloads revealed structural patterns and artifacts consistent with AI-assisted code generation.


Rather than standard developer documentation, multiple scripts contained conversational, step-by-step reasoning notes. These notes explained the code’s logic to the operator who provided the initial instructions. Their presence suggests that the code was either copied directly from an AI prompt output or deployed by an automated AI agent.


In addition, we identified several common characteristics that are consistent with AI-operated attacks, such as:


- Section headers in scripts and shell commands, which AI uses to analyze the output faster
- Extensive use of Base64-encoded commands
- Seamless switching between different technologies throughout the attack, including PHP, JavaScript, Bash and Python


Figure 1 shows snippets of code from scripts used by the attackers that contained AI-generated comments.


Figure 1. Snippets of code containing comments, indicating the use of AI.


## Dropping Multiple Web Shells for Initial Access


To gain access and maintain a persistent backdoor into the host networks, the attackers deployed a variety of web shells on the targeted Linux servers. These were a combination of custom and open-source web shells found on GitHub. Figure 2 shows interactive web shell activity from the php-fpm


parent process.


Figure 2. Interactive web shell activity, as shown in Cortex XDR.


To achieve persistence, the attackers modified the auto_prepend_file value across all PHP configurations under the directories /etc/php/


and /opt/plesk/php/


. These directories store all default PHP configuration files and[Plesk](https://www.hostinger.com/tutorials/what-is-plesk/) (web hosting control panel) configuration files. Any file that is specified in the modified auto_prepend_file


value will automatically load and execute before any other PHP script runs.


In one instance, the attackers deployed a malicious PHP web shell as a file named /usr/lib/php/plesk_sys_driver.php


to appear legitimate. They also modified the auto_prepend_file


to load the malicious web shell to ensure persistence. Figure 3 shows the attacker-deployed PHP script, including the original inline comments.


Figure 3. Malicious PHP script used to deploy a web shell and modify the auto_prepend_file


of every configuration file under /etc/php/


and /opt/plesk/php/


.


## Credential Harvesting Techniques


The attackers used multiple methods to gather credentials in the targeted environments, including:


- Editing the .bashrc


file
- Inserting malicious lines of code into PHP scripts
- Scanning the network for cleartext passwords


### Hijacked .bashrc File


The attackers replaced the[.bashrc](https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/bashrc-file-in-linux) file with a copy containing a malicious command that steals victims’ passwords. In one instance, they created an alias for the sudo


command that was designed to execute each time a user attempted to run it. The malicious command:


- Displays a prompt for the user to insert their password (mimicking the standard system authentication prompt)
- Captures the inserted password
- Writes it to the attackers’ log file


The harvested password is then passed to the legitimate sudo


command for execution, leaving the victim unaware of the underlying interception. The attackers named the log file Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt


, to mimic legitimate SolarWinds activity in the environment. We have no evidence of SolarWinds systems and infrastructure being compromised during this operation; the attackers misused the organization’s name as an evasion method.


Figure 4 shows the command hijacking technique inside the .bashrc


file.


Figure 4. Snippet of the .bashrc


file, showing the command used to hijack the sudo command.


### PHP Credential Logger


The attackers inserted a line of code into a PHP login page — most likely targeting a database authentication routine — to harvest admin credentials. If an administrator logs in, the code forwards the username and password to the attackers’ log file. Figure 5 shows a snippet of a PHP script including the code added by the attackers.


Figure 5. Code snippet of a PHP script that was inserted with a credential logger.


### Scanning for Cleartext Passwords


The attackers searched for email, SMTP and database passwords inside configuration files and command history files. Figure 6 shows an example of commands that the attackers used to search for cleartext passwords.


Figure 6. Searching for cleartext passwords in files, as seen in Cortex XDR.


## SysGoRAT Malware


The attackers deployed a custom-developed, multi-platform remote access Trojan (RAT) written in Go, first observed under the benign file name sys-control-client


. We named this malware SysGoRAT. This malware supports cross-platform execution on Windows and Linux and employs multiple persistence methods to maintain long-term access.


The malware established a command and control (C2) connection over WebSocket to wss://<addr>/ws


. This WebSocket address defaults to a hardcoded IP address 104.194.158\[.\]65:443


, which the malware operator can modify via a command-line parameter at execution. SysGoRAT supports a fixed set of seven command types, described in Table 1.


**Action** **Behavior**


command


Executes arbitrary commands via /bin/sh -c


(Linux) or cmd /C


(Windows)


control


Dispatches one of four sub-actions (seeControl Sub-Actions in Appendix A )


list_dir


Lists directory content


shell_input


Creates an interactive shell session


proxy_connect


Establishes a TCP connection to an arbitrary target


proxy_data


Relays data bidirectionally to an established proxy connection


proxy_close


Terminates and removes a proxy session


Table 1. SysGoRAT command types.


The malware’s sub-actions provide additional capabilities and persistence methods, detailed inAppendix A .


The attackers renamed the binary on disk to blend in, using different benign names on targeted endpoints, including:


- sys-control-client


- pip2.7


- ea_install


- ./semanage

## Targeting Mailboxes for Social Media Account Access


The attackers targeted official government mail servers to steal emails and facilitate access to external social media accounts.


In this operation, the attackers enumerated the /var/qmail/mailnames/


directories for several domains and counted the number of emails stored in specific users’ Maildir/cur/


directories to identify targets.


Next, the attackers searched for social media-related emails. They deployed a PHP script, named search_social.php


, that searched for specific keywords in email headers and displayed the results in a user-friendly format. Figure 8 shows the first part of the script.


Figure 8. A PHP script that searched for social media emails.


The script then parsed the response and displayed the exact file path, social media account email sender, recipient and subject.


Figure 9 demonstrates the expected output.


Figure 9. Expected output from the script.


After identifying the specific emails they wanted to exfiltrate, the attackers attempted to generate a bash script named zip_mails.sh


that would iterate through users’ directories and compress their emails into ZIP archives. Figure 10 shows this command.


Figure 10. Command used to exfiltrate entire mailboxes.


This bash script is intended to exfiltrate an entire mailbox rather than a specific social-media-related file identified by the previously analyzed script. In this particular instance, we found that the script contained syntax errors, such as a broken variable assignment user=\\;)


and would fail upon execution.


We found indications that the attackers also intended to exfiltrate multiple databases and steal highly sensitive government data. The data exfiltration techniques the attackers used are detailed inAppendix B .


## Defense Evasion and Anti-Forensics Attempts


A core component of the attackers’ playbook involved anti-forensics techniques, specifically:


- Attempting to disable endpoint protections
- Tampering with logs
- [Timestomping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1070/006/)
- Disguising malicious activity
- Deleting residual artifacts to hinder post-incident analysis


This section details the specific evasion techniques and cleanup commands the attackers used to cover their tracks.


### Disabling Endpoint Protection


One of the techniques the attackers used for defense evasion was an attempt to disable security protection devices on the compromised hosts. As Figure 11 shows, the attackers executed bash scripts that use the Linux commands pgrep


and pkill


to attempt to terminate Cortex XDR-related processes on infected systems.


Figure 11. Snippets of code from a script used in an attempt to terminate Cortex XDR.


These attempts were successfully detected and mitigated by Cortex XDR, with telemetry confirming that endpoint protections were not suppressed.


### Removing Scripts After Execution


Throughout the campaign, the attackers ensured that single-use scripts were removed after execution by formulating a single command that:


- Wrote the script to disk
- Executed the script
- Removed the script using rm


Figure 12 shows an example of this procedure as executed by the attackers.


Figure 12. A one-line command used to write, execute and remove a malicious PHP script.


### Timestomping


For scripts that were meant for long-term use, the attackers used timestomping.


They used the command touch -t


to change the access and modification time of malicious files, to make them appear as if they were created long before the attack started. The goal of this technique is to evade analysis by misleading analysts into believing the file is unrelated to malicious activity, due to its creation time predating the attack timeline.


### Disguising Activity as Red Team Operations


In several instances, we observed the attackers employing planted deception techniques to mislead post-incident analysis. They attempted to disguise their activity as a red team operation, by using operational indicators such as the key RedTeamOps2025


in one of the malicious scripts, and pentest123


as a password for a user the attackers created.


### Cleaning Up Logs and Residual Files


Following the exfiltration attempts, the attackers initiated a full cleanup of log files and malicious residual files on the systems. This cleanup included attempts to delete logs related to:


- Authentication
- Command history
- Email activity
- Operating system (OS)
- Web server
- Active PHP user sessions


Figure 13 shows the execution of shell commands to delete various log files from the system.


Figure 13. Shell commands used to delete log files from the system, as seen in Cortex XDR.


Following the mass log deletion, the attackers executed several automated cleanup commands and scripts, and verified that any evidence of the exfiltration was deleted.


Figure 14 shows one of the attackers’ cleanup scripts, including the original inline comments. The script attempts to delete various logs across the system for a second time and to remove any files from /tmp/


, where the attackers stored malicious scripts.


Figure 14. A snippet of the attackers’ cleanup script used to clean log files from evidence.


After the cleanup phase, the attackers attempted to verify the removal of evidence, checking whether IP addresses they used were removed from system log files, as Figure 15 shows.


Figure 15. A snippet of the attackers’ “verify” script, used to verify the deletion of logs.


Additional commonly used TTPs that the attackers leveraged throughout the campaign are detailed inAppendix B .


## Conclusion


This campaign demonstrates how attackers are combining traditional post-exploitation techniques with AI-accelerated workflows to target governmental Linux server infrastructure. By leveraging AI to rapidly generate, adapt and deploy operational scripts, the attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 maintained a fast pace of operation while minimizing manual developer overhead.


The attackers behind this activity exhibited a deep understanding of the Linux OS, employing techniques such as:


- Global PHP configuration hijacking for persistent access
- Command-line credential harvesting and privilege escalation using different shells


Alongside open-source utilities, their toolkit featured custom tools, including a multi-platform Go RAT and custom vulnerability scanners.


The attackers also maintained a thorough cleanup strategy to thwart forensic analysis, by erasing system logs and attempting to disable endpoint protections. Despite these evasion efforts, endpoint security controls effectively neutralized their activity. Cortex XDR detected and prevented the process termination attempts targeting the agent.


Attackers continue to adopt AI to streamline payload development and scale their campaigns.


Comprehensive visibility into Linux servers, databases and environments remains critical to countering attackers’ efforts and strengthening enterprise security.

## Appendix A: SysGoRAT Sub-Actions


First observed as sys-control-client


, SysGoRAT is a custom RAT developed by the attackers. The SysGoRAT malware had seven available command types, each with additional control


sub-actions.


### Control Sub-Actions


When the C2 server sends a control message, SysGoRAT triggers one of four specific operational actions.


**Action** **Behavior**


**shell_start**


Spawns an interactive /bin/bash


process


**screenshot**


Captures the current display as an image and returns it to the C2


**download**


Reads a specified file, optionally compresses it with gzip


, and exfiltrates it to the C2


**persist**


Installs persistence using one of six supported methods (see next table)


Table 2. SysGoRAT control


sub-actions.


### Persist Sub-Actions


The persist


action, triggered by the malware’s control


message, supports six different installation methods for cross-platform environments. All methods use artifact names designed to masquerade as legitimate software.


**Method** **Operating System** **Behavior**


**systemd**

; writes a unit (service) file to /etc/systemd/system/sys-update.service


; reloads and enables the service


**cron**


Linux Creates a crontab


entry with a five-minute execution interval


**registry**

and adds a Run key to HKCU


**schtasks**

**complex**

## Appendix B: Analysis of Additional CL-UNK-1211 TTPs


The following section provides an analysis of additional TTPs associated with the CL-UNK-1211 activity cluster. The TTPs described in this appendix are more common in the broader threat landscape than those discussed previously.


### ​​Privilege Escalation Using Open Source Tools


After gaining access to Linux servers, the attackers escalated their privileges. They started by deploying and executing an open-source tool called[LinPEAS](https://github.com/peass-ng/PEASS-ng/tree/master/linPEAS) to check for local privilege escalation paths. Next, they used another open-source tool —[PwnKit](https://github.com/ly4k/PwnKit) , a self-contained exploit for[CVE-2021-4034](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2021-4034) — in an attempt to gain root privileges on the system.


Once the attackers obtained root privileges, they deployed various binaries with the goal of maintaining root access:


- A renamed legitimate Python 3 interpreter:
The attackers used the Python 3 interpreter and renamed it to .libpython-helper


to execute shell commands with high privileges. They achieved this by using the Python commands os.setuid(0)


and os.setgid(0)


, which set root privileges for the shell.Following is an example of a command used:

### Reconnaissance


The attackers leveraged a variety of reconnaissance techniques to identify and map high-value servers across compromised networks.


#### Network Scanning and Database Enumeration Using PHP Scripts


The attackers used multiple PHP scripts to conduct reconnaissance of the target networks. The scripts were used to scan the network for SQL servers, enumerate databases, and enumerate various domain artifacts. These artifacts included users, computers and open shares. Figure 19 shows one of the scripts the attackers used to scan for SQL servers.


Figure 19. Malicious PHP script used to scan for SQL servers.


#### CVE-2025-55182 (React2Shell) Vulnerability Scanner


The attackers deployed a custom vulnerability scanner written in Go that scans for servers vulnerable to[CVE-2025-55182](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-55182) (React2Shell). Figure 20 shows the “Help” output of the scanner.


Figure 20. The “Help” output of the CVE-2025-55182 (React2Shell) vulnerability scanner.


### Propagating in the Environment


To bypass internal firewalls and extend their access beyond the initially compromised web servers, the attackers employed a combination of database features, custom malware and open-source proxy tools. These methods enabled the attackers to bypass firewalls, route traffic into the network and execute commands across multiple servers.

#### SSH-Based Persistency


The attackers achieved SSH-based persistence by injecting an SSH public key into the compromised user’s authorized_keys


file. This establishes passwordless remote shell access. Following is the command sequence the attackers executed to install the SSH backdoor:


1. Ensure the hidden .ssh


directory exists
2. Restrict directory access only to the owner (using chmod 700


)
3. Append the malicious public key to the authorized_keys


file
4. Set strict permissions on the authorized_keys


file

### Additional Proxy Tools


The attackers deployed a variety of tunneling and proxy tools, while employing multiple techniques to maintain persistence and evade detection:


- **revsocks** : The attackers deployed the open-source tool[revsocks](https://github.com/kost/revsocks) , a reverse SOCKS5 tunneling tool with SSL/TLS and proxy support.
- **pysoxy** : The tool set also included[pysoxy](https://github.com/MisterDaneel/pysoxy/) , an open-source Python SOCKS proxy script used to route traffic.
- **GSocket and gs-netcat:** The attackers misused[Global Socket](https://www.gsocket.io/) , a framework designed to solve NAT and firewall traversal problems. They deployed the framework’s binary, gs-netcat


, which forces the internal host to establish an outbound connection to the public relay server ( gsocket\[.\]io


).
This binary was stored in /dev/shm/.gs-10085/


and executed under the disguised process name \[kcached\]


(mimicking a kernel cache thread), alongside the binary gs-dbus


(mimicking the D-Bus system). Execution parameters were passed via the environment variable ( GSOCKET_ARGS


) to hide them from process monitoring, and the spawned sessions were configured with HISTFILE=/dev/null


to prevent shell command history from being logged to disk.


### Additional Data Exfiltration Attempts


The attackers used a combination of methods to extract sensitive data. We observed how they dumped entire database contents into compressed local archives before attempting to exfiltrate them to their C2 infrastructure. They also misused legitimate file-hosting platforms to blend the outgoing data with standard web traffic.


Exfiltration attempts began with attackers using the echo


command to print small data samples directly to the terminal, using TOP


clauses to limit the output. They subsequently attempted a structured dump, writing four tables, each capped at 100 rows, to a local SQLite database named dump.sqlite
